title: PHOEBI: An Open-World Benchmark for Multi-Label Bacterial Identification in Phase-Contrast Microscopy
claim: Models that excel on seen combinations collapse on unseen ones, while simple frozen-feature methods hold up and detect novel classes.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right: sample image, arrow dumbbell plot, two bar charts
description: The figure has three panels. On the left, a row of six colored circular species labels (bs, bt, mx, ka, fj, pf) sits above a brownish phase-contrast microscopy image with small bacteria. The caption below reads "PHOEBI: 6 species × 40 mixtures". The centre panel is titled "Compositional generalization gap on PHOEBI". It shows a dumbbell-style arrow plot of per-sample F1. Red arrows run from open circles near 1.0 down to filled circles between about 0.45 and 0.65, one for each of nine supervised backbones and for DINOv2 MIL. Three green methods labelled A, B and C show small changes (+0.08, +0.09, −0.05). The right panel has two horizontal bar charts. Open-set AUROC compares residual (grey, 0.44) with k-NN (green, 0.70). Novel-class cluster accuracy compares greedy (grey, 0.44) with SK K=1 (green, 0.50). The long red downward arrows draw the eye first.
caption: PHOEBI at a glance. Left: a phase-contrast field from a culture of all six species. Centre: each arrow runs from a model’s F1 on mixtures seen in training (open circle) to its F1 on mixtures it has never seen (filled circle), so a long downward arrow marks a model that does not carry over to new mixtures. Right: the same frozen features, with no further training, flag images that hold an unseen species (top) and gather them into a new class (bottom). Green marks the methods we adopt, and red and grey mark the alternatives they are compared with.
abstract: Optical microscopy lets us watch living bacteria in real time without stains or labels, and it remains the standard instrument for identifying species across clinical, environmental and industrial microbiology. Yet real samples rarely hold a single species. They arrive as mixtures and sometimes carry an organism no model has ever seen. What happens when a model trained on familiar mixtures meets one it has never encountered? No benchmark has asked this of phase-contrast images, so we built one. \textbf{PHOEBI} brings together 120,000 phase-contrast images of 40 mixtures of six bacterial species that we cultured and imaged ourselves, and it holds whole mixtures out of training so that every test is a combination the model has never seen. The answer is sobering. Classifiers that are nearly perfect on the mixtures they know collapse on new ones, and no choice of backbone or pretraining rescues them. The features turn out to be sound and the failure lies in how the evidence within each image is pooled. A culture looks the same everywhere, and decoders built on this simple fact hold steady where large networks fail even though one of them is never trained by gradient descent. The same features go further still. They notice when a species outside the catalogue appears, and the simplest way of giving it a class of its own proves the most effective while leaving the known species almost untouched. PHOEBI turns the mixed culture, the everyday case at the bench, into a measurable target for open-world recognition.
